title: Service Boundaries
description: Define clear service boundaries using domain-driven design, bounded contexts, and team ownership alignment. Learn how to split a monolith into services that are loosely coupled and independently deployable.

data.text: Service boundaries determine how your system is split into independent parts. Good boundaries make teams faster, failures isolated, and deployments safer. Bad boundaries create distributed monoliths — systems that are harder to operate than the monolith they replaced.
Senior engineers define service boundaries by understanding the business domain, not just the technical stack.

A bounded context is a clear boundary within which a particular domain model is defined and applicable. The word "customer" might mean a paying subscriber in the billing context and a newsletter reader in the marketing context. Each context has its own model, and the boundary between them is where translation happens.

data.text: Coupling measures how much one service depends on another. Cohesion measures how closely related the responsibilities inside a service are. The goal is low coupling and high cohesion.

cards.title: Low Coupling
cards.description: Services depend on each other through stable contracts, not internal implementation.
pros: Changes in one service rarely break others
Faults are contained within one service
cons: May need more infrastructure for communication

cards.title: High Cohesion
cards.description: All the logic inside a service relates to a single business capability.
pros: Code is easier to understand and maintain
Changes are localized to one team
cons: May duplicate small utilities across services
Requires discipline to avoid scope creep

cards.title: High Coupling
cards.description: Services share databases, call deep internal methods, or require synchronous chains.

cards.title: Low Cohesion
cards.description: A service handles multiple unrelated responsibilities.
cons: Code becomes a confusing mix of concerns
Teams step on each other's changes
Hard to test or deploy safely

data.text: There is no perfect formula for splitting a system. These heuristics help you find boundaries that work in practice.

data.title: Decomposition Heuristics
items: Split by business capability: payments, inventory, notifications, search
Align services with team ownership: each service should have one primary team
Separate fast-changing parts from stable parts: the checkout flow changes often; tax calculation changes rarely
Isolate data with different scaling needs: user profiles are small and frequent; audit logs are large and append-only
Put security-sensitive logic in its own service with strict access controls

data.title: Anti-Pattern Warning
data.text: Avoid splitting by technical layer alone (API layer, business logic layer, data access layer). This produces a distributed monolith with the worst of both worlds: the complexity of microservices and the tight coupling of a monolith.

Conway's Law states that organizations design systems that mirror their communication structure. If your teams are organized by function (frontend team, backend team, database team), your system will likely have functional layers instead of business capabilities. Reorganize teams first if you want to reorganize services.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Bounded contexts define where a domain model applies and where it must be translated
Low coupling and high cohesion are the goals of every service split
Decompose by business capability, not by technical layer
Align services with team ownership to reduce coordination overhead
Conway's Law means your org chart shapes your architecture
data.takeaway: Service boundaries are business decisions expressed in code. Understand the domain first.

items.question: How many services is too many?
items.answer: Start with fewer services. Every service adds operational overhead: deployment, monitoring, debugging, and communication. Split only when a service becomes too large for one team to manage safely.

items.question: What if two services need the same data?
items.answer: Duplicate the data. Each service owns its own copy and updates it through events or API calls. Shared databases create tight coupling that defeats the purpose of microservices.

items.question: Can I fix bad boundaries after launch?
items.answer: Yes, but it is expensive. Merging services is easier than splitting them. Invest time upfront in event storming or domain workshops to get boundaries right the first time.

data.title: Event Storming a Food Delivery App
data.description: Map out the key events in a food delivery app: order placed, restaurant notified, driver assigned, food picked up, delivered, rated. Identify bounded contexts and propose service boundaries for each. List the trade-offs of your split.
data.expectedOutcome: A diagram of bounded contexts, a list of proposed services, and a short analysis of coupling and cohesion in your design.
